questions.title: Benign tumours show a mature cell population
questions.question: A benign tumour usually shows:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood-borne spread is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.B: Correct. A benign tumour is usually composed of a mature, well-differentiated cell population that closely resembles its tissue of origin, without blood or lymphatic spread, extensive necrosis, or numerous mitotic figures. These other four features instead characterise a malignant tumour, whose growth outpaces its blood supply and whose cells divide rapidly and abnormally.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphatic spread is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extensive necrosis, from outgrowing its blood supply, is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Many mitotic figures reflect the rapid, abnormal division of malignant, not benign, cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that a benign tumour usually shows a mature cell population, distinguishing it from the blood/lymphatic spread, necrosis and high mitotic activity of a malignant tumour.

questions.title: A malignant ulcer has an indurated base
questions.question: A malignant ulcer is characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. A malignant ulcer is characterized by an indurated (hard) base, produced by infiltrating malignant tissue. This is distinct from a punched-out edge, more typical of an ischaemic or gummatous (syphilitic) ulcer, surrounding congestion, or a healthy floor, none of which is the defining feature of malignancy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A punched-out edge is more typical of an ischaemic or gummatous ulcer, not the defining feature of a malignant ulcer, which is instead its indurated base.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Surrounding congestion is not the defining feature of a malignant ulcer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A healthy floor is not characteristic of a malignant ulcer, whose base is instead indurated by infiltrating tumour.

questions.learning_objective: State that a malignant ulcer is characterized by an indurated base, distinguishing it from a punched-out edge, surrounding congestion or a healthy floor.

questions.title: Neoplasia is autonomous, parasitic growth
questions.question: Neoplasia is an autonomous growth characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. Neoplasia is defined as an autonomous, uncontrolled new growth that, once established, persists independently of the stimulus that initiated it, has no useful function to the host, and escapes normal biological growth control -- behaving parasitically by drawing nutrition from the host without contributing anything useful in return. This is what "parasitic" means in the classic definition of neoplasia, distinguishing it from a normal, controlled, functionally useful, stimulus-dependent tissue response.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neoplastic growth is autonomous of a continuing stimulus, not dependent on one persisting.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neoplastic growth serves no useful function to the host, unlike a normal, physiological tissue response.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neoplastic growth escapes normal biological growth control, rather than remaining subject to it.

questions.learning_objective: State that neoplasia is an autonomous growth that behaves parasitically toward the host, without a sustaining stimulus, useful function, or biological control.
questions.module_subject: AUN-MPT-104 > Pathology > Neoplasia: definition and classification

questions.title: A malignant ulcer's edge is raised and everted
questions.question: The edge of a malignant ulcer is:

explanations.A: Correct. The edge of a malignant ulcer is raised and everted, rolled outward, produced by the proliferating malignant tissue at its margin. This is distinct from a sloping edge, typical of a healing or traumatic/venous ulcer, an undermined edge, classically a tuberculous ulcer, or a punched-out edge, typical of an ischaemic or gummatous ulcer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A sloping edge is typical of a healing or traumatic/venous ulcer, not a malignant one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An undermined edge is classically a tuberculous ulcer's feature, not a malignant one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A punched-out edge is typical of an ischaemic or gummatous (syphilitic) ulcer, not a malignant one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Rolled over" is not the standard descriptive term used for a malignant ulcer's edge in this teaching scheme; the correct term is raised and everted.

questions.learning_objective: State that a malignant ulcer's edge is raised and everted, distinguishing it from the sloping, undermined and punched-out edges of other ulcer types.

questions.title: Malignant nuclei show abnormal mitosis
questions.question: The nuclei of malignant cells show:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Malignant nuclei are typically enlarged, not normal in size.
explanations.B: Correct. The nuclei of malignant cells show abnormal mitotic figures, atypical, sometimes tripolar spindle patterns, reflecting the disordered, excessive cell division that drives malignant growth. This is unlike normal nuclear size, a normal nucleus-to-cytoplasm (N/C) ratio, normochromatism, and uniform nuclear shape, which are instead features of benign or normal cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malignant nuclei typically show an increased, not normal, nucleus-to-cytoplasm (N/C) ratio.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Malignant nuclei are typically hyperchromatic, not normochromatic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Malignant nuclei typically show pleomorphism (variation in shape), not uniform shape.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant cell nuclei show abnormal mitotic figures, distinguishing this from the normal size, N/C ratio, chromatin staining and shape of benign or normal nuclei.

questions.title: Angioma is the uncapsulated benign tumour
questions.question: Which of these benign tumours is uncapsulated ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibroadenoma, like most benign tumours, grows slowly enough to compress and form a surrounding fibrous capsule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neurofibroma is not the option this teaching point marks as the uncapsulated example; angioma is the one the source keys as correct.
explanations.C: Correct. Most benign tumours -- fibroadenoma, chondroma and lipoma among them -- grow slowly enough to compress and form a surrounding fibrous capsule. Angioma, a vascular benign tumour or proliferation of blood vessels, characteristically lacks this true capsule, growing instead as an uncapsulated network of vessels within the surrounding tissue. This makes angioma the uncapsulated example among the five options given.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chondroma, like most benign tumours, grows slowly enough to compress and form a surrounding fibrous capsule.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipoma, like most benign tumours, grows slowly enough to compress and form a surrounding fibrous capsule.

questions.learning_objective: Identify angioma as the uncapsulated benign tumour among fibroadenoma, neurofibroma, chondroma and lipoma.
